title: Modules and error handling
summary: ES modules versus CommonJS (static graph, live bindings, run-once caching, cycles and the TDZ, default versus named, dynamic `import()`, type-only imports, interop), then errors: `Error` subclasses, `cause`, `finally`, `unknown` in `catch`, async failures, Result types and where retries belong.
prerequisiteNotes: ts-promises-async: a rejected promise only reaches a `try/catch` that awaits it, `Promise.allSettled` never rejects, and retry wraps `return await op()` in a loop. This lesson decides which failures deserve a throw, which deserve a Result, and which deserve a retry.
objectives: Contrast CommonJS and ES modules: run-time `require` versus a static graph, copied values versus live bindings, synchronous versus async-capable loading.
Explain why a module body runs once, in what order a graph evaluates, and what a circular import sees (partial exports in CommonJS, a TDZ `ReferenceError` in ESM).
Know what default versus named exports, dynamic `import()` and `import type` do at run time, and name the common CJS/ESM interop traps.
Throw `Error` subclasses with a proper `name` and a `cause`, and predict how `finally` interacts with `return` and `throw`.
Narrow a `catch (e)` variable of type `unknown` into an `Error` safely, and know which async failures a `try` can and cannot see.
Choose between exceptions and a typed `Result` union, and say where retries belong and which errors must never be retried.

concepts.title: CommonJS versus ES modules
concepts.body: **CommonJS** (CJS, Node's original system) is a function call: `require(path)` runs at the moment it is reached, synchronously, can take any computed string, and returns whatever object the module put on `module.exports`. **ES modules** (ESM, the language standard) are declarations: `import` and `export` must sit at the top level with string-literal specifiers, so the engine can parse the whole dependency graph, link every import to its export **before any code runs**, and load files asynchronously (which is what enables top-level `await`). Static structure is also why bundlers can tree-shake ESM and why a misspelled named import fails at link time instead of producing `undefined` later. ESM code is always in strict mode, has no `require`, `module` or `__dirname`, and uses `import.meta.url` instead.

concepts.title: Live bindings versus copied values
concepts.body: An ESM import is a **live, read-only view** of the exporting module's variable, not a copy. If `math.mjs` runs `count++`, every importer sees the new `count`; assigning to an imported name is a `TypeError` at run time (and a TypeScript error). CJS has no such link: `module.exports = { count }` copies the current number into a property, so later `count++` inside the module is invisible to anyone who destructured it. Objects are shared either way (both see mutations of the same object); the difference is only about the **binding**. One subtle ESM case: `export default expr` evaluates `expr` once and exports that value, so `export default count` is **not** live, while `export { count as default }` is. The code simulates both models with a getter (live) and a plain property (copy).
concepts.code:
let count = 0
function inc(): void { count++ }

const esmView = { get count() { return count } }  // like `import { count }`
const cjsView = { count, inc }                    // like `module.exports = { count, inc }`

cjsView.inc()
console.log(esmView.count)  // 1: the getter reads the variable
console.log(cjsView.count)  // 0: a copy taken at export time

concepts.title: Evaluation order: every module runs once
concepts.body: A module's top-level code runs **once per resolved specifier** (per file path in CJS, per URL in ESM); every later `require` or `import` gets the **cached** instance. That is why a module is a natural singleton (a config object, a connection pool) and why side effects at the top level happen exactly once. ESM evaluates in three phases: **load and parse** the whole graph, **link** imports to exports, then **evaluate** in post-order depth-first order, so dependencies run before the modules that import them and siblings run in the order their `import` statements appear. CJS evaluates lazily, depth first, as each `require` call is reached. Two paths that resolve to two different files (two copies of a package in `node_modules`) produce two instances, which breaks singletons and `instanceof`.

concepts.title: Circular imports see half-built modules
concepts.body: When `a` requires `b` and `b` requires `a`, the loader must hand `b` **something** for `a`, because `a` has started but not finished. CJS returns `a`'s `module.exports` object **as it is right now**: properties assigned later are missing (`undefined`), and if `a` later **replaces** `module.exports` with a new object, `b` keeps the stale empty one forever. ESM links bindings before running anything, so `b` gets real bindings to `a`, but `a`'s `let`, `const` and `class` exports are in the **temporal dead zone** until their declaration runs: reading one throws `ReferenceError`. Exported `function` declarations are initialised during linking, so calling them across a cycle works. Fixes: read the import lazily inside a function, or move the shared piece into a third module both can depend on.
concepts.code:
// a.mjs                                // b.mjs
import { b } from './b.mjs'               import { a, helper } from './a.mjs'
export const a = 'A'                     export const b = 'B'
export function helper() { return 'h' }  helper()          // fine: hoisted function
                                         console.log(a)    // ReferenceError: a is in the TDZ

concepts.title: Default versus named, dynamic `import()`, type-only imports
concepts.body: Named exports keep one name across the codebase, so renames, auto-imports and grep work; a default export is just a binding called `default` that each importer names freely. Many teams prefer named exports for that reason. Dynamic `import(specifier)` is an expression that returns a **promise** of the module namespace object (`ns.default` holds the default export); it works in both ESM and CJS, accepts a computed string, and is how you lazy-load or code-split. `import type { User }` (or `import { type User }`) is **erased** entirely: types do not exist at run time, so a type-only import never loads or runs the module. Under `verbatimModuleSyntax`, TypeScript keeps every import not marked `type` exactly as written, so marking type imports is required, and a side-effect import like `import './polyfills'` is always kept.

concepts.title: Interop pain points between CJS and ESM
concepts.body: In Node, a package is ESM when its `package.json` has `"type": "module"` or the file ends in `.mjs`, and CJS for `.cjs` or no `type`. ESM can `import` a CJS file: the default import is its `module.exports`, and named imports work only when Node can statically detect the property names. CJS loading ESM traditionally had to use `await import()`; `require()` of an ES module threw `ERR_REQUIRE_ESM`, and only recent Node versions (22.12 and later) allow it for modules without top-level `await`. Code compiled from ESM to CJS marks itself with `exports.__esModule = true` and puts the default on `exports.default`, which is why TypeScript's `esModuleInterop` emits a helper so `import x from 'cjs-lib'` gets `module.exports`. Relative ESM imports in Node need the file extension. A package loaded once as CJS and once as ESM is the **dual package hazard**: two instances, two singletons, failing `instanceof`.

concepts.title: Throw `Error` objects, subclass them, chain with `cause`
concepts.body: JavaScript lets you `throw` **any** value (`throw 'oops'`, `throw 404`), but only `Error` objects carry a `stack`, a `message` and a `name` that tools understand, so throw `Error`s and convert anything else at the boundary. Subclass `Error` for failures callers handle differently, and **set** `name`, because the inherited `name` is `'Error'` and that is what logs print. With ES2015+ output, `instanceof` works on subclasses; with an ES5 target it did not without `Object.setPrototypeOf(this, new.target.prototype)`. ES2022 added `cause`: `new Error(message, { cause })` wraps a low-level error without losing it, and Node prints the chain. `AggregateError` (from `Promise.any`) holds many errors in `.errors`.

concepts.title: `catch (e)` is `unknown`: narrow before you use it
concepts.body: Because anything can be thrown, TypeScript's `strict` mode enables `useUnknownInCatchVariables` (since 4.4): the catch variable is `unknown`, so `e.message` does not compile until you narrow. You may annotate it only as `unknown` or `any`, never as a specific class, because TypeScript cannot know what was thrown. Narrow with `instanceof Error` (or your subclass) and handle the rest with a normaliser like `toError(e)` that wraps strings and odd values in an `Error` with `cause` set to the original. If you do not need the value, `catch { ... }` (optional binding, ES2019) is cleaner. Rethrow what you cannot handle instead of swallowing it.

concepts.title: `finally` always runs and can override the outcome
concepts.body: `finally` runs after the `try` (or `catch`) finishes by any route: falling through, `return`, `throw`, `break` or `continue`. If the `finally` block itself **returns** or **throws**, that new completion **replaces** the pending one: a `return` in `finally` silently discards an exception in flight and overrides an earlier `return`. So use `finally` only for cleanup (release a lock, clear a timer, close a handle) and never `return` from it. The value of `return x` is computed **before** `finally` runs, so reassigning `x` there does not change what is returned. In `async` code, `try { return await p } finally { ... }` runs cleanup after `p` settles; without the `await`, it runs too early.

concepts.title: Async errors: what a `try` can and cannot see
concepts.body: A `try/catch` catches a rejection only if the promise is **awaited inside** the `try`. A promise you start and do not await (fire-and-forget) rejects later, outside the `try`, and with no handler it becomes an **unhandled rejection**: Node 15+ crashes the process and browsers fire `unhandledrejection`. A `throw` inside a `setTimeout` callback or an event listener runs on a later task, so no surrounding `try` sees it either. To collect many failures without fail-fast, use `Promise.allSettled` and inspect each `status`. Treat process-level hooks (`process.on('unhandledRejection')`) as last-resort logging, not error handling.

concepts.title: Exceptions or a `Result` type?
concepts.body: A function's TypeScript signature says nothing about what it throws, so callers forget to handle it. A **Result** (or Either) union such as `{ ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: E }` puts **expected** failures in the return type: the compiler forces the caller to check `ok` before touching `value`, and `E` can be a precise union of domain errors. Use Results for outcomes the caller is expected to handle (validation, parse failure, not found, a payment declined). Keep exceptions for bugs and broken invariants, and for failures nobody nearby can fix (out of memory, a misconfigured service), where unwinding to a top-level handler is right. Convert at boundaries: wrap a throwing API once with `tryAsync` and pass Results inward.

concepts.title: Where retries belong
concepts.body: Retry only **transient** failures (timeouts, connection resets, 429 and 503 responses) and never deterministic ones (validation errors, 400, 404): retrying those only repeats the failure. Retry only operations that are **idempotent** or carry an idempotency key, or a retried payment charges twice. Retry at **one layer**: if the client, the gateway and the service each try 3 times, one user action can become `3 * 3 * 3 = 27` calls against a struggling dependency. Bound the loop with a maximum attempt count and an overall deadline, use exponential backoff with jitter, honour `Retry-After`, and let a circuit breaker stop calling a dependency that is clearly down. Make retryability explicit, for example a `retryable` flag on your error class, instead of guessing from message strings.

walkthrough.title: Build a CJS-style loader with a cache
walkthrough.body: A `require` implementation needs a **cache** keyed by module name. On a call: if the name is cached, return the cached exports object, even if that module is still running (that is the cycle case). Otherwise create an empty exports object and put it in the cache **before** running the module body, then run the body, which may call `require` recursively for its own dependencies, and finally fill in the exports and return them. Caching after the body runs is the classic bug: a cycle then never finds the module in the cache and recurses until the stack overflows, which is exactly what real Node avoids by registering the module first.

walkthrough.title: Solve the task in three moves
walkthrough.body: First write the inner `load(name)` with the cache check, then the existence check that throws `Error("Cannot find module 'x'")` (use `Object.hasOwn` so names like `toString` are not found on the prototype). Second, register an empty exports object, log `run name`, and for each dependency call `load` and log what it returned, printing `?` when `value` is still unset; use `??`, not `||`, so an empty-string value prints as empty rather than `?`. Third, wrap the top-level `load(entry)` in `try/catch`, narrow the `unknown` error, and append `error: ...` to the log. Mention that real Node also deletes a module from the cache when its body throws, so a later `require` retries it.

task: Write `runLoader(modules, entry)`, a tiny CommonJS-style loader. `modules` maps a name to `{ deps, value }`. Loading a module logs `"run name"`, then loads each dependency in order and logs `"name got dep=v"` where `v` is that dependency's exported `value`, or `?` if it is not set yet; after its dependencies it exports its own `value`. Each module body runs **at most once**: a repeat load returns the cached exports, and in a cycle that means the **partially built** exports. Loading a name that is not in `modules` throws `Error("Cannot find module 'name'")`; catch it at the top, append `"error: <message>"` and stop. Return the log.
hints: The cycle only terminates if a module is in the cache from the moment its body starts. Create the empty exports object and `cache.set` it before running anything.

Use `got.value ?? '?'` so an unset value prints `?` but an empty string stays empty, check existence with `Object.hasOwn(modules, name)`, and wrap the top-level `load(entry)` in `try/catch` with an `instanceof Error` check.
checklist: A module is registered in the cache before its body runs, so a cycle returns partial exports instead of overflowing the stack.
A shared dependency in a diamond runs once; a repeat load logs `got` lines but no second `run`.
An unset value prints `?`, while an empty-string value prints as empty (`??`, not `||`).
A missing module, including a missing entry, appends `error: Cannot find module '...'` and stops.
The catch variable is treated as `unknown` and narrowed with `instanceof Error`.
pitfalls: Destructuring a CommonJS export (`const { count } = require(...)`) and expecting it to update when the module changes it; only ESM imports are live.
Writing `export default count` and expecting a live binding; the default export of an expression is a one-time value.
Replacing `module.exports` at the end of a module in a cycle, so the other side keeps the stale empty object forever.
Reading an imported `const` at the top level of a module in an import cycle, which throws a TDZ `ReferenceError`.
Forgetting to set `name` on an `Error` subclass, so logs and `String(e)` say `Error` instead of the class.
Returning from `finally`, which silently swallows the exception in flight.
Calling an async function inside `try` without `await` and believing the `catch` protects it.
Retrying 400s or non-idempotent operations, or stacking retries at several layers so one call becomes dozens.

extraPractice.title: Normalise anything thrown
extraPractice.prompt: Write `toError(value: unknown): Error` and use it in `describeThrown(values)`, which throws each value, catches it and returns `"name: message"` per value. An `Error` is returned as is. A string becomes `new Error(value)`. An object with a string `message` becomes an `Error` with that message, and it also copies a string `name` if there is one. Anything else becomes `Error("Non-error thrown: <JSON>")`, falling back to `String(value)` when `JSON.stringify` gives `undefined` or throws. Keep the original value as the `cause` of every new `Error`.
hints: Narrow step by step: `instanceof Error`, then `typeof value === 'string'`, then `typeof value === 'object' && value !== null && 'message' in value && typeof value.message === 'string'`.
`JSON.stringify(undefined)` returns `undefined` and `JSON.stringify` of a cyclic object throws, so wrap it in a small `safeString` with `try/catch` and `?? String(value)`.
checklist: The parameter is `unknown`, not `any`, so every branch narrows before reading properties.
`{ message: 5 }` is not treated as error-like: the message must be a string.
Every newly created `Error` carries the original thrown value as `cause`.

extraPractice.title: tryAsync and a Result union
extraPractice.prompt: Declare `type Result<T, E = Error>` as a union discriminated on `ok` (`{ ok: true; value: T }` or `{ ok: false; error: E }`) and write `tryAsync<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<Result<T>>`, which **never rejects**: it captures rejections **and** synchronous throws from `fn`, normalising the reason with `toError`. `runAll(specs)` (provided) starts every task through `tryAsync`, waits for all of them and returns `{ lines, failed }` with `ok value` or `fail message` per task in input order. Tasks may fulfil, reject with an `Error`, reject with a bare string, or throw before returning a promise.
hints: Make `tryAsync` an `async` function and put `await fn()` inside its `try`: the call itself is then inside the `try`, so a synchronous throw is caught too.
In the `catch`, return `{ ok: false, error: toError(caught) }`; the caller can then narrow with `if (r.ok)` and TypeScript knows which field exists.
checklist: `Result` is a discriminated union, so reading `value` without checking `ok` is a compile error.
A synchronous throw from `fn` becomes `{ ok: false }` instead of escaping `tryAsync`.
A bare string rejection is wrapped by `toError`, so `error.message` is always a string.

followUps.question: Your service's config module is imported by 40 files. How many times does its top-level code run, and when would it run twice?
followUps.answer: Once per resolved module: every importer gets the cached instance, which is why a module works as a singleton. It runs twice when the same code is reached through two different resolutions: two copies of a package in `node_modules`, the same file loaded once as CJS and once as ESM (the dual package hazard), different query strings in ESM URLs, or a test runner that resets the module registry between tests. Symptoms are two connection pools or `instanceof` failing across the two copies.

followUps.question: How would you break a circular import between `orders` and `customers`?
followUps.answer: First ask why it exists: usually both need a shared type or helper, which belongs in a third module both depend on. Type-only cycles are harmless because `import type` is erased. If a runtime cycle must stay, make the access lazy (read the import inside a function, not at module top level) or inject the dependency at startup. Tools such as `madge` or ESLint's `import/no-cycle` catch cycles in CI.

followUps.question: When would you return a Result instead of throwing?
followUps.answer: When the failure is an expected outcome the immediate caller must decide about: invalid input, a parse failure, a missing record, a declined payment. The union makes it visible in the type and the compiler forces the check. Throw for bugs and broken invariants, and for failures only a top-level handler can deal with. Mixing styles in one layer is the real problem, so convert at the boundary (wrap a throwing library once) and keep one style inside.

followUps.question: Why does `catch (e: Error)` not compile, and what do you do instead?
followUps.answer: Anything can be thrown, so TypeScript allows only `unknown` or `any` on the catch variable; a specific type would be an unchecked lie. Narrow inside the block with `instanceof Error` or a subclass, use a normaliser like `toError(e)` when you need an `Error` regardless, and rethrow what you do not handle. For a typed error channel, return a Result instead of throwing.

takeaways: CJS `require` runs at call time and copies values; ESM builds a static graph first and imports are live, read-only bindings.
A module body runs once per resolved path; ESM evaluates dependencies first, in post-order.
Cycles expose half-built modules: partial `module.exports` in CJS, TDZ `ReferenceError`s in ESM.
`import type` is erased, dynamic `import()` returns a promise of the namespace, and CJS/ESM interop has real traps.
Throw `Error` subclasses with a `name` and a `cause`; never `return` from `finally`.
`catch (e)` is `unknown`: narrow it or normalise it with `toError`, and await inside the `try`.
Use a Result union for expected failures, exceptions for bugs, and retry only transient, idempotent work at one layer.

diagrams.title: CommonJS versus ES modules
diagrams.alt: Two panels. On the left, CommonJS: main.js calls require at run time, which synchronously runs the a.js body; it assigns a plain module.exports object, and destructuring that object copies the values into local constants. On the right, ES modules: the engine parses static import specifiers into a module graph with linked bindings, evaluates dependencies first and once, and an imported name always reads the exporter's current value.
diagrams.caption: CommonJS is a run-time function call that hands back copies; ESM links a static graph first and imports stay live.

after.label: ES modules: static graph, live bindings

diagrams.title: Loading an ES module graph: main imports a, a imports b
diagrams.alt: Timeline of five phases. First main.mjs, a.mjs and b.mjs are fetched and parsed by following static import specifiers. Then all bindings are linked while no code has run. Then b.mjs, the leaf, is evaluated, followed by a.mjs, and finally main.mjs; a later import of a.mjs reuses the cached instance.
diagrams.caption: ESM loads and links the whole graph before running anything, then evaluates leaves first; each module body runs exactly once.

events.label: Fetch main.mjs, read its static import specifiers, then fetch and parse a.mjs and b.mjs
Create every module's bindings and wire each import to its export; no code has run yet
The leaf runs first (post-order depth-first); its top-level code runs exactly once
a.mjs runs after its dependency b.mjs has finished
The entry runs last; any later import of a.mjs or b.mjs reuses the cached instance

diagrams.title: A CommonJS cycle hands out a half-built module
diagrams.alt: Sequence diagram with main, a.js, b.js and the module cache. main requires a; a is cached as an empty object and starts running; a requires b; b requires a again and the cache returns a's partial, still empty exports, so b sees undefined; b finishes and returns its complete exports to a; a finishes and returns to main.
diagrams.caption: The loader registers a module before running it, so a cycle gets the partial exports instead of looping forever.

messages.label: partial a: {}
messages.note: a has not finished, so b reads undefined for a.x.

messages.label: a.x set, full exports
messages.note: In ESM the order is the same, but reading a's let or const early throws a TDZ ReferenceError.

diagrams.title: Narrowing an unknown catch variable
diagrams.alt: Decision flow starting at catch (e) where e is unknown. If e is an instance of Error, use it as is. Otherwise, if it is a string, wrap it in new Error with cause set to e. Anything else is stringified safely and then wrapped the same way.
diagrams.caption: Narrow first; whatever is not an Error gets wrapped in one, with the original kept as cause.

steps.text: The catch variable is `unknown` under `strict`: nothing can be read from it until it is narrowed.
`instanceof Error` covers built-ins and your subclasses; use the error as it is.
A thrown string is common in old code: wrap it so the rest of the program always sees an `Error`.
Numbers, objects and `undefined` are stringified safely (`JSON.stringify` can throw or return `undefined`) and wrapped, keeping the original as `cause`.

diagrams.title: Throwing versus returning a Result
diagrams.alt: Two panels. On the left, a caller calls parse(text), whose signature says it returns Config; on bad input it throws, which is not in the type, and if uncaught the error unwinds to a crash or a 500. On the right, parse(text) returns Result of Config: a valid input gives ok true with the value, an invalid input gives ok false with a ParseError, and the caller must check ok before using either.
diagrams.caption: A Result puts the expected failure into the type, so the compiler makes the caller handle it.

after.label: Result: failure is part of the type

diagrams.title: Inside a require() with a cache
diagrams.alt: Flow of a require call. require(name) asks whether the name is in the cache. If yes, it returns the cached exports, which may be partial. If not, it registers an empty exports object in the cache before the body runs, runs the body, which may call require again for its dependencies, then fills the exports and returns them.
diagrams.caption: Registering the empty exports before running the body is what makes repeat loads cheap and cycles terminate.

steps.text: `require(name)` first looks the name up in the cache.
A hit returns the cached exports object immediately; the body never runs again.
A miss registers an empty exports object first, then runs the module body.
The body requires its dependencies; in a cycle one of them comes back here and hits the half-built entry.
When the body finishes, the exports are filled in and returned; everyone holding that object now sees the values.

exercises.typeChecks:
type Equal<A, B> = (<T>() => T extends A ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends B ? 1 : 2) ? true : false
type Expect<T extends true> = T
type _1 = Expect<Equal<Parameters<typeof toError>[0], unknown>>
type _2 = Expect<Equal<ReturnType<typeof toError>, Error>>

predict.explain: The getter reads the variable every time, like an ESM live binding, so it sees 1. The plain property copied 0 when the object was built, like `module.exports = { count }`, and never changes.
The second call hits the cache: the body runs once and both callers get the very same exports object, which is why modules behave as singletons.

choices: b sees a.ready=undefined, a sees b.ready=true
b sees a.ready=true, a sees b.ready=true
a sees b.ready=true, b sees a.ready=true
predict.explain: `a` starts, is cached empty, and loads `b`. `b` loads `a` again and gets the half-built object, so it sees `undefined`; `b` then finishes before `a` reads it.

A `return` inside `finally` replaces the pending completion, here the `return` from `catch`. It would equally swallow an exception, which is why returning from `finally` is a lint error in most configs.
`name` is inherited from `Error.prototype`, so it stays `'Error'` unless the subclass sets it. `instanceof` works because the output targets ES2022 (with an ES5 target it would have been `false`).
`const config` exists but is in the temporal dead zone until its line runs, so reading it throws. An ESM import cycle produces the same error when a module reads another's `const` export too early.
`JSON.parse` throws a `SyntaxError`; wrapping it with `{ cause: e }` keeps it reachable as `e.cause`, so the outer handler gets both the high-level message and the root cause.

lab.tip: When asked about modules, draw the graph and say the three words **load, link, evaluate**, then explain that a module runs once and cycles see half-built exports. For error handling, state your policy before coding: which failures are expected (return a Result), which are bugs (throw), which are transient (retry at one layer, with backoff and a deadline). Interviewers are checking that you have a policy, not just `try/catch`.
